content.abbreviations: CO = cardiac output; BP = blood pressure; ECMO = extracorporeal membrane oxygenation; RV = right ventricle/ventricular.
content.fluid_management: Epinephrine is used in cardiac arrest. If central venous pressure is low, modest (~250–500 mL) fluid challenge can be used as it may increase cardiac index in patients with acute PE. Volume loading can over-distend the RV and reduce systemic CO. Aggressive volume expansion is of no benefit and may worsen RV function. Cautious volume loading may be appropriate if low arterial pressure is combined with absence of elevated filling pressures. Assessment of central venous pressure by ultrasound imaging of the IVC or by central venous pressure monitoring may help guide volume loading. If signs of elevated central venous pressure are observed, further volume loading should be withheld.
content.vasopressors_and_inotropes: Use of vasopressors is often necessary, in parallel with (or while waiting for) pharmacological, surgical, or interventional reperfusion treatment. Norepinephrine can improve systemic haemodynamics by improving ventricular systolic interaction and coronary perfusion without causing a change in PVR; its use should be limited to patients in cardiogenic shock. Dobutamine may be considered for patients with PE, low cardiac index, and normal BP, but increasing cardiac index may aggravate ventilation/perfusion mismatch. Experimental data suggest levosimendan may restore RV–pulmonary arterial coupling in acute PE by combining pulmonary vasodilation with increased RV contractility, but no evidence of clinical benefit is available.
content.vasodilators: Vasodilators decrease PAP and PVR but may worsen hypotension and systemic hypoperfusion due to lack of specificity for pulmonary vasculature after systemic (i.v.) administration. Small clinical studies suggest inhaled nitric oxide may improve haemodynamic status and gas exchange in patients with PE, but no conclusive evidence for clinical efficacy or safety is available to date.
content.mechanical_support_and_oxygenation: Temporary mechanical cardiopulmonary support, mostly venoarterial ECMO, may be helpful in patients with high-risk PE and circulatory collapse or cardiac arrest. Survival has been described in case series, but no randomized controlled trials test efficacy and safety of these devices in high-risk PE. Use of ECMO is associated with high incidence of complications and increased bleeding risk related to vascular access, especially in patients undergoing thrombolysis.
content.clinical_recommendations_summary: Avoid aggressive volume loading in acute high-risk PE; consider modest fluid challenge only if low CVP and low arterial pressure without elevated filling pressures. Use vasopressors (norepinephrine) in cardiogenic shock; consider inotropes cautiously. Consider ECMO as temporary support in selected high-risk cases, acknowledging limited evidence and high complication risk.
